newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-TOP MEN STRUGGLE, WOMEN RACE TO VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-TOP MEN STRUGGLE, WOMEN RACE TO VICTORY.

text.p: Former men's champions Jim Courier and Pete Sampras struggled to find their form in the Australian Open on Thursday as the top women sailed into the third round of the tournament.

World number one Sampras conceded he had entered the danger zone of the US$7.6 million grand slam after a hesitant four-set win over Romanian Adrian Voinea, while Courier had five bruising sets against Slava Dosedel of the Czech Republic.
Sampras said he felt out of sorts at the start of his centre court struggle with 48th ranked Voinea, who played with nothing to lose.
"I didn't play too well," top seed Sampras told reporters after pulling himself together to wrap up the match 3-6 6-2 6-3 6-2 with 14 aces.
"I was just a little bit flat, I was missing a little bit and got off to a bad start," Sampras added.
He now faces in-form Australian Mark Woodforde, a semifinalist here last year, for a place in the final 16.

Woodforde, who has an impressive list of upset wins over the past 12 months, hopes to repeat the feat of compatriot Mark Philippoussis who last year threw Sampras out of the Open in the third round before a wildly partisan crowd.
"He is very capable of beating me," said Sampras of the 28th ranked Woodforde.

Courier, a former world number one climbing back up the rankings after a disappointing 1996, was at his belligerent best at the end of a three-an-a-half-hour tussle with Dosedel, ranked world number 67.
"I think this year I have played as well as I've ever played," said Courier, who has a history of clawing his way through grand slam draws with five-set wins.
By contrast, fifth seed Thomas Muster of Austria and 10th seed Albert Costa of Spain powered into the third round in straight sets, as did the top women's seeds.

Swiss starlet Martina Hingis and eighth seed Irina Spirlea were both straight sets winners, while second seed Arantxa Sanchez Vicario did not have time to raise a sweat before her opponent retired hurt.
Sanchez Vicario was a game ahead three minutes into the match when Belgian Stephanie de Ville twisted an ankle and had to be taken from the court in a wheelchair.

Germany's Anke Huber, whose mother added her name to the injury list when she mysteriously collapsed here on Wednesday, also won through, although Italy's Francesca Lubiani gave the world number five a fright by taking the first set 6-4.
"She's doing fine and she's coming back this afternoon from hospital and everything was okay," said Huber, whose second-round match was postponed because of the incident.
Hingis, a multi-millionaire at 16, said she played "almost perfect tennis" in the second set against American Lisa Raymond to triumph 6-4 6-2.
Czechoslovak-born Hingis has been in the headlines this week for a five-year deal with an Italian sportswear label worth up to US$12 million if she ousts Graf from the number one spot.
But Hingis complained after her win that too much had been made of the deal and she might only get US$1.4 million a year.
"I would really like to be as rich as they make out in the newspapers. That would be great," Hingis told reporters.
"I don't get all this money. That's the problem."
